=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Buyer’s position

**Do not accept this package as drafted.** The Seller combines broad disclosure and deemed Buyer knowledge with a narrow claims regime, while leaving material completion risks unresolved. That could leave Wattlebridge acquiring liabilities and impaired assets with little effective recourse.

This review is based on the supplied update and Disclosure Letter, not the underlying SPA or DD documents. Their precise wording must be checked before agreeing amendments.

## Material issues and recommended pushback

### 1. Liability limitations would undermine core protections

The proposed general warranty cap is **AUD 4.8 million**, with an **AUD 25,000 de minimis**, **AUD 250,000 deductible basket**, and **18-month notification period**.

Those figures require commercial negotiation, but the principal concern is the proposal to extend limitations to **all Claims**, including fundamental warranties, indemnities and contractual obligations.

**Push back:**
- Confine the general warranty regime to expressly identified general warranties.
- Give title, capacity and authority warranties separate protection: seek a cap of at least the purchase price, no de minimis or basket, and a substantially longer claim period.
- Give tax warranties and the tax indemnity a separate regime aligned with applicable assessment and recovery periods, including an appropriate notification buffer.
- Negotiate appropriate longer protection for material IP ownership risks.
- Exclude specific indemnities, completion and price-adjustment obligations, and debt-discharge obligations from general warranty restrictions unless expressly negotiated otherwise.
- Include express carve-outs for fraud and fraudulent concealment, and preserve rights that cannot lawfully be excluded.

For general warranties, seek a lower de minimis, aggregation of related claims and a **tipping basket**, under which qualifying losses become recoverable from the first dollar once the basket is exceeded. Seek at least 24 months for notification and ensure timely notified claims survive until resolved. Check for any separate, short deadline to commence proceedings.

**Why:** A defect in ownership of the shares, an unpaid completion obligation or an identified indemnity risk should not receive the same protection as an ordinary business warranty claim.

### 2. General disclosure and deemed knowledge could hollow out the warranties

The Seller seeks to disclose everything “contained or referred to” in the data room, statutory registers and public records. Clause 8.3 then excludes matters the Buyer or its advisers knew—or could have discovered.

**Push back:**
- Require **fair disclosure**, with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter and reasonably assess its implications.
- Reject blanket disclosure of documents merely referred to, inaccessible material and unrestricted public-record disclosure.
- Identify and preserve a fixed, indexed data-room archive. Require subsequent disclosures to be specifically identified and subject to agreed consequences, not automatic acceptance.
- Delete constructive or “discoverable” knowledge. Prefer no Buyer-knowledge exclusion; any compromise should be limited to actual knowledge of named individuals, without deemed adviser knowledge or a duty to investigate.
- Ensure disclosure and knowledge do not defeat specific indemnities or completion obligations.

**Why:** Providing information is not the same as allocating the resulting financial risk. The Seller’s reservations do not resolve the disclosed problems.

### 3. Bluefen: written consent alone may be insufficient

Bluefen represents approximately **AUD 3.6 million, or 30%, of FY26 revenue**. The letter expressly confirms that neither final consent nor evidence of satisfaction of associated conditions has been supplied.

**Push back:**
- Make effective Bluefen consent a Buyer-waivable condition precedent.
- Require satisfaction of all relevant clause 11.3 conditions and confirmation that consent is effective for this transaction.
- Do not accept materially adverse pricing changes, termination rights, fees or other concessions without Buyer approval.
- Require prompt delivery of correspondence, active progress obligations and a long-stop termination right.

**Why:** “Reasonable endeavours” regulates the Seller’s efforts; it does not ensure the Buyer acquires the business with this key customer relationship intact. The update’s assertion that consent is “addressed” is not supported by the disclosure.

### 4. Riverlark: repayment and security release must be coordinated with Completion

Approximately **AUD 3.2 million** remains outstanding. A promise to provide a release after Completion is inconsistent with a properly protected debt-free acquisition.

**Push back:**
- Obtain a current payout letter covering principal, interest, fees and all secured obligations.
- Apply the necessary completion proceeds directly to repayment, with the amount reflected in the equity-price calculation.
- Require an effective release of security and guarantees at Completion through an agreed, enforceable discharge arrangement.
- Verify relevant registrations and obtain evidence of their removal promptly afterwards.

**Why:** Administrative removal of a registration may follow Completion, but substantive release should not depend on an unsecured post-completion promise.

### 5. Completion bonuses: ensure the Seller bears the full cost

The **AUD 420,000** bonuses are omitted from the draft funds flow. Calling them “a matter for the Seller” does not prevent the acquired company from having to pay them.

**Push back:**
- Review the payment triggers, employment conditions and legal obligor.
- Allocate the full agreed Seller-borne cost through a debt-like deduction, transaction-expense adjustment or direct Seller payment.
- Determine applicable superannuation, payroll tax, withholding and other on-costs.
- Provide for contingent amounts that crystallise later and prohibit double counting through working capital or other adjustments.

**Why:** Otherwise Wattlebridge could pay the stated purchase price and then fund an additional transaction-triggered liability.

### 6. Ironquay: the issue is IP ownership, not just an unpaid invoice

The record indicates that transfer of SOW3 materials depends on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. An **AUD 180,000 open balance** is evidence requiring investigation, not conclusive proof of non-payment. There is no payment receipt or confirmatory assignment.

**Push back:**
- Reconcile all relevant fees and obtain independent payment evidence.
- Require an effective confirmatory assignment or acknowledgement of ownership, supported by chain-of-title checks and necessary third-party permissions.
- If material IP remains unresolved, make satisfactory resolution a completion condition.
- Replace the payment-only indemnity with protection for losses arising from the identified ownership defect, including reasonable defence, replacement and remediation costs, subject to expressly negotiated terms.

**Why:** Paying an invoice alone may not cure every ownership or usage-right defect. An indemnity capped at the invoice amount may bear little relationship to the business impact.

### 7. Export/privacy incident: investigate; do not assume either harmlessness or a confirmed breach

The preliminary record concerns a link sent to an unintended external address and potentially **1,240 records**. It does not establish access, exact scope, notification obligations or loss.

**Push back:**
- Require immediate containment, preservation of logs and a properly documented investigation.
- Establish link permissions, access/download evidence, affected information and applicable contractual and statutory obligations.
- Assess any notification duties promptly, including under the Australian notifiable data breaches regime if applicable.
- Require Buyer consultation on material remediation and communications, without delaying legally required action.
- Seek a specific indemnity for the pre-completion incident and related reasonable response costs and third-party liabilities, with penalties covered only to the extent legally permissible.

**Why:** The Seller has no evidentiary basis to dismiss materiality, but the Buyer should not describe this as a confirmed notifiable breach either.

### 8. Sandbar renewals: assess the AUD 330,000 commitment collectively

Three related **AUD 110,000** renewals should be assessed together. The disclosure does not establish whether they are ordinary-course, unavoidable, accrued or terminable.

**Push back:**
- Obtain the contracts, renewal deadlines, cancellation rights, service periods and commercial rationale.
- Apply interim operating covenants and consent thresholds to related commitments in aggregate.
- Determine the correct treatment under the agreed working-capital, debt and transaction-expense definitions.

**Why:** Neither automatic acceptance as ordinary operating expenditure nor automatic deduction as debt is justified on the current evidence.

### 9. Title and other contractual requirements need verification—not assumptions

**Shares:** The register is evidence of registered ownership, not complete proof of unencumbered title. Verify the issued capital, constitution, options and other rights, transfer restrictions, encumbrances and required approvals. Require proper transfer deliverables and robust title warranties.

**Office lease:** On the supplied account, this is a notification obligation, not a landlord-consent condition. Check and comply with the actual notice requirement.

**Mossvale:** An assignment restriction does not automatically apply to a share sale. Review the full contract for a separate change-of-control provision or other relevant trigger before requiring consent.

### 10. Exclusive-remedy and non-reliance clauses require substantive narrowing

Clauses 9.3, 12.8 and 20.5 must not override the negotiated risk allocation.

Preserve express warranties, indemnities, price adjustments, completion obligations and appropriate equitable remedies. Reject language that purports to eliminate all misleading-conduct or other statutory claims regardless of enforceability. Under Australian law, non-reliance wording can affect reliance and causation, but it does not automatically exclude mandatory statutory liability.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **Completion protections:** Effective Bluefen consent and conditions; Riverlark repayment and release; satisfactory resolution of material Ironquay ownership issues.
2. **Protect the economics:** Reconcile the funds flow with the AUD 24 million debt-free/cash-free deal, including bonuses, on-costs and relevant adjustments.
3. **Restore meaningful recourse:** Narrow disclosure, knowledge, exclusive-remedy and limitation provisions; establish separate fundamental, tax and specific-indemnity regimes.
4. **Resolve factual uncertainty:** Investigate the export incident, supplier commitments and title evidence without overstating what the record proves.
5. **Secure recovery:** Consider retention, escrow or other credit support for unresolved exposures, particularly if the Seller may distribute sale proceeds.

**Bottom line:** A disclosed risk is not necessarily an accepted risk. Material exposures should be cured before Completion, reflected in price, or expressly retained by the Seller with effective recovery protection.
